specAnchors.text: draw and explain reaction profile diagrams showing Δ H and activation energy

primer.text: From Catalysts you already know that helpers open lower-energy routes through a reaction. This note draws those routes as reaction profiles, adding the peak that particles must clear before any product forms. Reading that peak, and the arrow for the overall change, is the skill this note builds.

modules.title: Reading reaction profiles
modules.opening: A reaction profile is the energy level diagram grown a curve: it follows the energy as bonds strain, peak and settle. This lesson names the two features examiners want labelled, the enthalpy arrow and the energy hurdle.
keyPoints: Reaction profiles show the relative energies of reactants and products and how energy changes as the reaction progresses.
The height difference between reactants and products represents the overall enthalpy change.
For an exothermic reaction the enthalpy value is negative and the arrow points downwards.
For an endothermic reaction the enthalpy value is positive and the arrow points upwards.
The climb from reactants up to the peak of the curve marks the energy needed to start reacting.

low.restatement: The profile line starts at the reactants, climbs over a hump and settles at the products. The hump is the energy hurdle for starting, and the height drop or climb from start to finish gives the overall change.
low.analogy: It is like a cross-country run: the race starts and finishes at set heights, but the hardest hill in between decides who can even complete the course.
low.examPointer: Label both the enthalpy change arrow and the activation energy rise when drawing a profile.

medium.restatement: A reaction profile traces energy from reactants over a peak to products, with the reactant-to-product gap giving the overall enthalpy change and the reactant-to-peak rise giving the energy hurdle for starting. Downward overall arrows carry negative values for exothermic reactions and upward arrows positive ones for endothermic.
medium.analogy: A theme-park ride climbs its biggest lift hill before any drops; the lift height is the activation energy and the net height change is the enthalpy change.
medium.examPointer: Mark Ea from reactants to peak and ΔH from reactants to products, with the sign matching the direction.

modules.title: Catalysts drawn onto the profile
modules.opening: A catalyst redraws the profile with a second, lower hump while the start and finish stay put. This lesson sketches that overlay and explains why the lower hump means a faster reaction.
keyPoints: Catalysts provide the reactants with an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.
A lower peak means a greater proportion of molecules have sufficient energy for an effective collision.
The catalysed reaction finishes faster than the same reaction without the catalyst.
The reactant and product levels on the profile are unchanged by adding a catalyst.
Reactions with low activation energy occur readily because little energy is needed to begin.

low.restatement: Draw the same start and finish, then add a smaller hump labelled as the catalysed route. More particles can clear the smaller hump, so the catalysed reaction runs faster even though the overall change is identical.
low.analogy: Two paths over the same hill: the tunnel route needs far less climbing, so more hikers finish per hour.
low.examPointer: Show both humps on one diagram and label the lower one as the catalysed pathway.

medium.restatement: The catalysed profile keeps the original reactant and product levels but offers a lower peak, so a greater proportion of molecules can achieve an effective collision. The catalysed reaction therefore completes faster while the overall enthalpy change stays exactly as before.
medium.analogy: Adding a chairlift does not move the mountain top, but far more skiers reach it each hour; the mountain is the reaction, the lift is the catalyst.
medium.examPointer: State that the peak drops, not the levels, and link the drop to a greater proportion of effective collisions.

glossary.definition: A diagram showing how energy changes as a reaction progresses, including the activation peak.
The minimum energy that reacting particles must have for a reaction to occur.
The energy difference between reactants and products, drawn as the arrow between the levels.
A collision with enough energy to form products, made more likely by a lower peak.
The lower-energy route through a reaction provided by a catalyst.

workedExample.prompt: a) Describe how a reaction profile shows the activation energy and the overall enthalpy change for an exothermic reaction. b) Explain how a catalyst appears on a reaction profile and why it increases the rate. c) What happens to the enthalpy change when a catalyst is added?
steps: a) The curve starts at the reactant level, climbs to a peak and settles at the product level below the reactants: the initial rise from reactants to the peak is the activation energy Ea, and the drop from reactants to products is the overall enthalpy change, which is negative for an exothermic reaction (a downwards arrow).
b) The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower peak: a greater proportion of molecules then have sufficient energy for an effective collision, so the rate increases.
c) The enthalpy change is unchanged — the reactant and product levels stay exactly where they were; only the peak is lowered.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Reactants-to-peak = Ea; reactants-to-products drop = ΔH (negative, exothermic). b) A lower catalysed peak means more effective collisions, so faster. c) Unchanged.
